sections.heading: 1. Key Expressions & Sentences Reviewed (Lessons 1–6)
points: Lesson 1: "Huyai kuno nekukasira!" — Come here quickly!
Lesson 2: "Amai vakati, "Chiuya kuno undibatsire."" — Mother said, "Come here now and help me."
Lesson 3: "Makorokoto nekubudirira kwenyu!" — Congratulations on your success!
Lesson 4: "Vhara musuwo zvakasimba kana uchibuda mumba." — Close the door firmly when you leave the house.
Lesson 5: "Svika kumba nenguva nhasi tisati tadya manheru." — Arrive home on time today before we eat dinner.
Lesson 6: "Dzoka kumusha nekukurumidza kana wapedza basa." — Return home quickly when you finish work.

sections.heading: 2. Core Shona Grammar Rules Consolidated
points: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Huyai'): Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]
Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Chiuya'): Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]
Celebrating Milestones with 'Makorokoto!': Makorokoto + ne- + ku-[verb] = Congratulations on [doing something]! (e.g., Makorokoto nekubudirira!)
Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Vhara'): Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]
Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('manheru'): Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Context & Practical Usage
points: Everyday Communication, Politeness & Community Life: In everyday Shona conversation (as in 'Come here quickly!'), speakers place a strong emphasis on politeness, patience, and consideration for others around them—whether asking for help ('ndinokumbirawo undibatsire'), speaking quietly when someone is resting or studying, or sharing news with family at the end of the day..
Household Cooperation, Politeness & Consideration at Home: Daily home life in Shona culture revolves around mutual assistance ('kubatsirana') and consideration for others in the household.

Celebrating Shared Success ('Makorokoto!'): Whenever someone passes an exam, starts a new job, welcomes a child, or achieves a goal, friends, neighbours, and family gather to say 'Makorokoto!' ('Congratulations!').

review_exercises.prompt: Review 1 — Greeting & Politeness: How do you say 'Good morning, did you wake up well?' to an elder?
review_exercises.explanation: 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning and 'mamuka zvakanaka here?' politely asks if they woke up well.

review_exercises.prompt: Review 1 — Polite Commands: Change the singular command 'Uya kuno!' ('Come here!') into the polite/plural form:
review_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' to an imperative verb stem ('uya' -> 'uyai') makes it plural or respectful.

review_exercises.prompt: Review 1 — Household Actions: Which verb means 'Close the window gently'?
Review 1 — Expressing Purpose: What does 'kuti tidye tese' mean in 'Ugosvika manheru kuti tidye tese'?
options: so that we may eat together
if you want to drink water
review_exercises.correct_answer: so that we may eat together
review_exercises.explanation: 'Kuti' + subjunctive 'tidye' ('that we eat') + 'tese' ('all of us / together') expresses purpose.

review_exercises.prompt: Review 1 — Sequence Commands: In 'Tora bhuku undipe', what does 'undipe' mean?
options: and put it on the bed

review_exercises.prompt: Review 1 — Translate this new review sentence: 'Ndapota gara pasi umirire amai.'
options: Please sit down and wait for Mother.
Please open the door and help Father.
Congratulations on finishing your work today.
Return home quickly before it rains.
review_exercises.correct_answer: Please sit down and wait for Mother.
review_exercises.explanation: 'Ndapota' = 'Please', 'gara pasi' = 'sit down', 'umirire amai' = 'and wait for Mother'.
